title: Ki Teitzei: the mother bird (Deuteronomy 22:6–7)
hook: send the mother bird away before taking the eggs, a command that promises long life

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elders of the nearest town: did we feed him, did we walk with him? Your line was the nearest town answers. Who did you check on? Today a new portion, and a nest by the road. Day five hundred seven.

The new portion is Ki Teitzei, when you go out, and it's packed. By the rabbis' count it holds more commandments than any other portion in the Torah, about seventy-four. Marriage, debts, lost property, fences, wages, animals. And tucked among them is a scene so small it's easy to miss. You're walking along a road, and there's a bird's nest in a tree or on the ground, with the mother sitting on the eggs or the chicks. It's the kind of moment that lasts a few seconds. The Torah stops for it.
screen: `KI TEITZEI: WHEN YOU GO OUT.` → `SEVENTY-FOUR COMMANDMENTS.` → `A NEST BY THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: The law: don't take the mother along with the young. Send the mother away first, and then you may take the eggs or the chicks. And the reward, in the old Jewish translation: "that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days." That promise is startling, because almost the only other commandment in the Torah with long life attached is honoring your father and mother. The greatest of family duties and a bird's nest by the road get the same reward. Why? Here the tradition doesn't speak with one voice, and it's worth hearing both. Maimonides, in his Guide for the Perplexed, says it's about compassion: animals feel grief, a mother bird's distress at seeing her young taken is real, and the Torah wants to spare her. Nachmanides says it's about us: the law trains people not to become cruel. But the Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, has a surprise. If a prayer leader says to God, your mercy reaches even to the bird's nest, they silence him. The Talmud explains: he turns God's commandments into mercy, when they are decrees. In other words, don't claim to know exactly why God commanded it. Do it because it's commanded. So one camp says the reason is compassion, another says don't presume a reason at all. Both camps send the mother away. And maybe that's the point of a tiny law with an enormous reward: the smallest act of care counts.
screen: `SEND THE MOTHER AWAY FIRST.` · `THE SAME REWARD AS HONORING PARENTS.` · `COMPASSION, SAYS MAIMONIDES.` · `A DECREE, SAYS THE MISHNAH.` · then, large: `SPARE THE MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle with one creature. Settle, and breathe. Think of the creatures you'll cross paths with today. A pet who wants attention. A spider in the bathtub. Birds at a feeder. A neighbor's dog that barks. Even the ant on the counter. Picture one of them, and picture a gentler way of meeting it than usual. Carrying the spider outside. Ten slow minutes with the dog. Water left out. Small. That's the scale of this law. The bell holds the time.
Ki Teitzei. When you go out. The portion with the most commandments in the Torah, and a nest by the road.
Your line: spare the mother. Today, be gentle with one creature in a way you'd usually not bother with. Day five hundred seven.

howItsDone: Shiluach haken, sending away the mother bird, is still practiced by some Jews, who seek out a nest of a kosher wild bird to fulfill it, and the debate over its reason is a classic of Jewish thought.
